jian:study:1.title: First Non-Avian Theropod (Dromaeosauridae, Microraptorinae) from the Bird-Bearing Lower Cretaceous Xiagou Formation of the Changma Basin, Gansu Province, Northwestern China (Annals of Carnegie Museum, 2026)

jian:abstract:1.title: First Non-Avian Theropod (Dromaeosauridae, Microraptorinae) from the Bird-Bearing Lower Cretaceous Xiagou Formation of the Changma Basin, Gansu Province, Northwestern China (abstract)

facts.statement: The genus Jian contains only one species, Jian changmaensis, which is known from a pectoral girdle and a partial forelimb.
facts.quote: J. changmaensis is the only species in the genus Jian, known from a pectoral girdle and partial forelimb.

facts.statement: Jian changmaensis is the first non-avian dinosaur described from the Xiagou Formation, following the discovery of over 100 bird fossils there.
facts.quote: After the discovery of more than 100 bird fossils in the formation, this specimen is the first non-avian dinosaur to be described from it.

facts.statement: Fossil material of Jian was discovered in 2008 in the Xiagou Formation near Changma village in northwest Gansu Province, China.
facts.quote: The Jian fossil material was discovered in 2008 in outcrops of the Xiagou Formation, part of the Changma Basin, near Changma village in northwest Gansu Province, China.

facts.statement: Ling-Qi Zhou and colleagues formally described Jian changmaensis as a new genus and species in 2026, designating specimen GSGM-D050 as the holotype.
facts.quote: In 2026, Ling-Qi Zhou and colleagues described Jian changmaensis as a new genus and species of microraptorine dinosaur based on these fossil remains, establishing GSGM-D050 as the holotype specimen.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen of Jian changmaensis is permanently housed in the Gansu Geological Museum under the accession number GSGM-D050.
facts.quote: The specimen is housed in the Gansu Geological Museum, where it is permanently accessioned as specimen GSGM-D050.

facts.statement: The fossil remains of Jian were first reported in a conference abstract in 2010.
facts.quote: The specimen was initially reported in a 2010 conference abstract.

facts.statement: The known fossil material consists of an articulated pectoral girdle and part of the forelimb, including the humerus, radius, and ulna.
facts.quote: It consists of an articulated portion of the skeleton, including the pectoral girdle (scapulocoracoid) and part of the forelimb (humerus, radius, and ulna).

facts.statement: Jian is considered a medium-sized microraptorine, larger than small Microraptor and Zhongjianosaurus but smaller than Sinornithosaurus and Changyuraptor.
facts.quote: Jian is regarded as a medium-sized member of the Microraptorinae with a size in between that of Wulong (known from an immature specimen), Zhongjianosaurus, and small Microraptor, and the larger Sinornithosaurus and Changyuraptor.

facts.statement: The firm co-ossification of the scapula and coracoid indicates that the holotype specimen belonged to a skeletally mature individual.
facts.quote: Based on the firm co-ossification of the elements of the pectoral girdle (scapula and coracoid, Zhou and colleagues identified the holotype as belonging to a skeletally mature individual.

facts.statement: Unique features of Jian changmaensis include a coracoid-to-humerus ratio greater than in any other microraptorine, distal humeral condyles primarily on the cranial surface, and a prominent foramen at the top of the radius in ventral view.
facts.quote: Autapomorphies (unique derived characters distinguishing it from other species) of Jian changmaensis include the ratio of the coracoid to the humerus (greater than in any other microraptorine), the distal condyles of the humerus primarily on the bone's cranial surface (in related species it is less cranially-oriented), and the presence of a prominent foramen at the top part of the radius when seen in ventral view (from below).

facts.statement: Accumulations of shattered bird bones, similar to owl pellets, have been found at the Xiagou Formation site where Jian fossils occur.
facts.quote: Several accumulations of shattered bird bones—reminiscent of the pellets regurgitated by modern owls—have been found in the Xiagou Formation site from which Jian is known.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that Jian may have produced the accumulations of shattered bird bones found at the locality, given it is the only non-bird there and one of the largest known microraptorines.
facts.quote: As the only non-bird from the locality, and as one of the largest known microraptorines, Jian may have been the producer of these bone masses.

facts.statement: Jian lived during the Early Cretaceous period, specifically the Aptian age.
The time range for Jian is estimated to be between 121.4 and 113.2 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Aptian to Aptian (121.4 to 113.2 million years ago)

facts.statement: Jian is classified as a microraptorine dromaeosaurid.
Phylogenetic analysis recovered Jian as a member of the dromaeosaurid subfamily Microraptorinae.
facts.quote: This analysis recovered Jian as a member of the dromaeosaurid subfamily Microraptorinae.

facts.statement: Phylogenetic analysis placed Jian in an unresolved polytomy with other derived microraptorines such as Hesperonychus, Microraptor, and Zhongjianosaurus.
facts.quote: Their 50% majority-rule consensus tree, which recovered better resolution than their strict consensus tree, placed it in an unresolved polytomy of derived microraptorines, including Hesperonychus, Microraptor, and Zhongjianosaurus.
